authored_against: Grade 3 science, elementary band. Keys state established science at this grade band; they are not extracted from the source, which states only a focus and generic objectives.

relationships: An observation is information taken in directly, through the senses or through a tool such as a hand lens, ruler, or thermometer.
An inference is an explanation of what an observation might mean; the same observation can support more than one inference.
An observation recorded at the time it is made is more reliable than one recalled later, because memory changes.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing observations as qualitative or quantitative is correct and so is describing them as words or numbers; neither wording is required.
disqualifying_errors: Recording an inference as an observation, such as writing 'the plant is thirsty' instead of 'the leaves are drooping'.
Claiming that an opinion about what happened counts as data.
Claiming an observation only counts if a tool was used; unaided senses give observations too.
topics.out_of_scope: Measurement uncertainty, instrument calibration, and statistical treatment of repeated observations belong to later grades and must not be required here.

relationships: A testable question is one that could be answered by observing something or by doing something and seeing what happens.
A testable question names something to change or look at and something to notice or measure.
Questions about what is best, prettiest, or fairest are not settled by a test on their own, because no observation decides them.
accepted_alternative_framings: A question phrased as 'what happens if', 'how does X affect Y', or 'which of these' can all be testable; no single sentence frame is required.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a question testable when no possible observation could answer it.
Claiming a question must begin with 'why' to be scientific.
Treating 'what does the book say' as a testable question about the natural world.
topics.out_of_scope: Naming independent and dependent variables, and formal hypothesis statements, are introduced later.

relationships: A model is a representation used to show or explain how something works: a drawing, diagram, physical build, or acted-out sequence.
Every model leaves something out. What it leaves out is a limitation of the model, not a mistake by the learner.
A model is judged by what it explains and predicts about the thing it stands for, not by how attractive it looks.
accepted_alternative_framings: A labelled drawing, a physical build, and a sequence of pictures are all models; the form the learner chooses is not a correctness question.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a model must look exactly like the real thing to be a good model.
Claiming a good model has no limitations.
Scoring a model on artistic quality rather than on what it explains.
topics.out_of_scope: Mathematical and computational models are later work.

fixed_facts: In a fair test only one thing is changed on purpose.
relationships: In a fair test one thing is changed on purpose and everything else that could affect the result is kept the same.
If more than one thing changes at once, you cannot tell which change caused the result.
Repeating a test gives more confidence in the result than a single try does.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a test fair when two or more conditions were changed at the same time.
Claiming a single trial proves a result.
Treating a result that disagrees with the prediction as a failed test; a fair test that disagrees with the prediction is still a good test.
topics.out_of_scope: Control groups by name, randomisation, and sample-size reasoning are later work.

fixed_facts: A measurement is incomplete without its unit.
relationships: A measurement has both a number and a unit; the number alone does not say how much.
The same quantity measured with the same tool by different people should agree closely, and a large disagreement is a signal to check the method.
Data recorded in a table with labelled columns can be compared; loose notes usually cannot.
accepted_alternative_framings: Metric and customary units are both acceptable, provided one system is used consistently within a comparison.
disqualifying_errors: Recording a bare number with no unit and treating it as a complete measurement.
Changing a recorded measurement afterwards so it matches a prediction.
Claiming a longer number is automatically a more accurate measurement.
topics.out_of_scope: Significant figures, uncertainty ranges, and error propagation are later work.

relationships: Criteria are what a successful solution must do; constraints are the limits it must work within, such as materials, cost, time, or safety.
The problem is defined before solutions are compared, so that every solution is judged against the same criteria.
A solution can meet every criterion and still be rejected because it breaks a constraint.
disqualifying_errors: Treating criteria and constraints as the same thing.
Judging a design best without stating what it was judged against.
Adding a new criterion after testing so that a preferred design wins.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted trade-off matrices and formal optimisation are later work.

fixed_facts: A force is a push or a pull.
relationships: A force is a push or a pull on an object, and it comes from an interaction between two objects.
A force has both a strength and a direction.
A force can start motion, stop motion, change speed, or change direction.
accepted_alternative_framings: Describing a force by an arrow, by words, or by a demonstration are all correct representations at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an object exerts a force on itself, or that a moving object carries a stored force inside it.
Claiming an object stopped because the force ran out, rather than because another force such as friction acted on it.
Describing a force by strength only, with no direction.
topics.out_of_scope: Newton's laws by name, the newton as a unit, and net-force arithmetic belong to later grades.

fixed_facts: Balanced forces do not change an object's motion; unbalanced forces do.
relationships: When the forces on an object are balanced, its motion does not change: at rest it stays at rest, and moving it keeps the same speed and direction.
When the forces on an object are unbalanced, its motion changes.
Balanced does not mean no forces are acting; it means the forces cancel each other.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an object sitting still has no forces acting on it.
Claiming balanced forces bring a moving object to a stop.
Claiming the larger or heavier object always wins in a push.
topics.out_of_scope: Vector addition, free-body diagrams, and quantitative net force are later work.

relationships: Motion that repeats regularly, such as a swing, a spinning wheel, or a ball rolling down the same ramp, can be observed, described, and used to predict what happens next.
A pattern is established by repeated observation; something seen once is not yet a pattern.
A pattern supports a prediction only while the conditions that produced it stay the same.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a single observation a pattern and predicting from it.
Predicting from a pattern after the conditions have been changed, without saying so.
Claiming a pattern explains why the motion happens; a pattern describes, it does not by itself explain.
topics.out_of_scope: Position-time graphs and the mathematics of periodic motion are later work.

relationships: If the pattern of an object's past motion is known and the conditions stay the same, its future motion can be predicted.
A prediction is stated before the observation; a statement made afterwards is an explanation, not a prediction.
A prediction that turns out wrong is evidence, and it is recorded as it was made.
disqualifying_errors: Rewriting a prediction after seeing the result.
Claiming a prediction is guaranteed rather than expected.
Predicting motion for conditions the observed pattern never covered.
topics.out_of_scope: Calculating a future position from speed and time is later work.

relationships: Distance and time are measured with tools and reported with units; two values can only be compared when they use the same unit.
Starting and stopping a timer by hand adds error to every trial, which is why several trials are taken.
A fair comparison of two motions uses the same starting point, the same finish point, and the same measuring method.
disqualifying_errors: Comparing distances recorded in different units without converting them.
Treating a single hand-timed trial as exact.
Changing the start or finish point between trials and comparing the results anyway.
topics.out_of_scope: Speed as distance divided by time is Grade 4 work and is not required here.

fixed_facts: Friction acts only between surfaces that are touching.
relationships: Friction is a force between surfaces that are touching, and it opposes sliding.
Under otherwise identical conditions, a rougher pair of surfaces produces more friction than a smoother pair.
Friction turns some of the energy of motion into thermal energy, which is why rubbed surfaces warm up.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming friction acts on an object when nothing is touching it.
Claiming friction is always a problem; friction is what makes walking, gripping, and braking possible.
Claiming a smoother surface always gives faster motion regardless of the other forces acting.
topics.out_of_scope: Coefficients of friction, and the static-versus-kinetic distinction by name, are later work.

fixed_facts: Magnets do not attract every metal. Aluminium and copper are metals and are not attracted.
relationships: A magnet exerts a force on some materials without touching them.
Magnets attract objects containing iron, nickel, or cobalt; they do not attract copper, aluminium, glass, plastic, or wood.
The magnetic force between a magnet and an object weakens as the distance between them increases.
accepted_alternative_framings: A learner who says 'magnetic materials' rather than naming iron, nickel, and cobalt is correct, provided the examples they give are right.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming magnets attract all metals.
Claiming a magnet has to touch an object to affect it.
Claiming the force is the same at every distance.
topics.out_of_scope: Magnetic domains, field-strength units, and electromagnets are later work.

fixed_facts: Like poles repel; unlike poles attract.
Every magnet has both a north and a south pole.
relationships: Every magnet has two poles, called north and south.
Like poles repel each other and unlike poles attract each other.
Cutting a magnet in half gives two magnets, each with two poles; a piece with only one pole is never produced.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming like poles attract.
Claiming a magnet can be cut to give a north-only piece.
Claiming the north pole of a magnet is stronger than its south pole.
topics.out_of_scope: Earth's magnetic field, polarity conventions, and magnetic declination are later work.

relationships: Magnetic and electric forces act between objects that are not touching.
Gravity also acts without contact.
The strength of a non-contact force depends on the distance between the objects and on properties of the objects themselves.
accepted_alternative_framings: Calling these 'forces at a distance' or 'non-contact forces' are both correct.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every force needs contact.
Claiming a non-contact force is equally strong at any distance.
Claiming magnetism and static electricity are the same force.
topics.out_of_scope: Fields as a formal representation, and inverse-square relationships, are later work.

fixed_facts: Opposite charges attract; like charges repel.
relationships: Rubbing certain materials together transfers electric charge from one to the other, leaving each object charged.
Objects with opposite charges attract each other; objects with the same charge repel each other.
A charged object can attract an uncharged object such as paper, hair, or a thin stream of water.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming rubbing creates charge out of nothing, rather than moving it from one object to the other.
Claiming static electricity and magnetism are the same thing.
Claiming an uncharged object cannot be attracted to a charged one.
topics.out_of_scope: Electrons by name, the conductor-insulator distinction, and current electricity are later work; a learner who uses them correctly is not wrong.

relationships: A cause-and-effect claim names what was changed and what changed as a result.
Two things happening at the same time does not on its own show that one caused the other.
Evidence for a cause comes from changing one thing and observing what follows.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming one event caused another only because they happened together.
Stating an effect with no named cause and calling it an explanation.
Reversing cause and effect without evidence about which came first.
topics.out_of_scope: Correlation coefficients, confounding by name, and controlled-variable vocabulary are later work.

relationships: A magnetic solution only works on materials the magnet actually attracts, so the material is part of defining the problem.
A design is tested against its stated criteria and constraints, not against how clever it seems.
A stronger magnet, or a smaller gap, gives the design a larger force to work with.
disqualifying_errors: Proposing a magnetic solution for a material magnets do not attract.
Declaring a design successful without testing it against the stated criteria.
Claiming a magnet works through any material without checking.
topics.out_of_scope: Electromagnet design and quantitative force calculations are later work.

fixed_facts: All organisms have life cycles that include being born or germinating, growing, reproducing, and dying.
relationships: All organisms have life cycles that include being born or germinating, growing, reproducing, and dying.
The particular stages differ between kinds of organism, but the overall birth-growth-reproduction-death pattern is shared.
Different kinds of organism take characteristically different lengths of time to complete a life cycle.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming some organisms never die.
Claiming every organism passes through the same stages, such as a larval stage.
Claiming an organism grows up into a different kind of organism.
topics.out_of_scope: Cell division, the genetics of reproduction, and alternation of generations are later work.

fixed_facts: In a flowering plant, pollination and fertilisation must occur before seeds form.
relationships: A flowering plant's cycle runs seed, germination, seedling, mature plant with flowers, pollination, then fruit and seed.
Seeds form after pollination and fertilisation; a flower that is never pollinated does not produce seed.
A seed contains a young plant and a store of food that supports early growth before the seedling has leaves of its own.
accepted_alternative_framings: Pollination by wind, water, insects, or other animals are all correct; the agent is not fixed.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a flowering plant produces seeds without pollination.
Claiming a germinating seed grows because the soil feeds it; early growth runs on the seed's own stored food.
Claiming plants take their food ready-made from the soil rather than making it themselves.
topics.out_of_scope: Photosynthesis chemistry, double fertilisation, and the cycles of non-flowering plants are later work.

fixed_facts: Complete metamorphosis is egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Incomplete metamorphosis is egg, nymph, adult, with no pupal stage.
relationships: Many insects undergo complete metamorphosis: egg, larva, pupa, adult.
Other insects undergo incomplete metamorphosis: egg, nymph, adult, with no pupal stage.
The larva and the adult of one insect can look completely different and eat different food, and are still the same individual organism.
accepted_alternative_framings: Caterpillar for larva and chrysalis or cocoon for the pupal stage are acceptable everyday names.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every insect passes through a pupal stage.
Claiming a caterpillar and the butterfly it becomes are two different organisms.
Placing the pupa before the larva in the sequence.
topics.out_of_scope: Hormonal control of moulting, and counting instars, are later work.

relationships: Comparing life cycles means matching stages that play the same role, not stages that share a name.
Organisms that look very different can share the same overall cycle pattern.
A difference between two life cycles is evidence about the organisms, not a fault in either of them.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an organism with a shorter life cycle is less developed or less successful.
Matching a plant's seed to an animal's adult stage as if they played the same role.
Claiming two organisms with different stage names cannot be compared.
topics.out_of_scope: Interpreting life-cycle similarity as evidence of relatedness is later work.

relationships: A life-cycle model shows the stages in order and shows that the cycle repeats.
A representation that ends at the adult stage shows a sequence, not a cycle.
The arrows in the model carry meaning: they show the direction of change over time.
accepted_alternative_framings: A circular diagram, a labelled set of pictures in order, or a built model are all acceptable forms.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing a life cycle as a straight line with no return to the first stage.
Leaving out a stage the organism actually passes through and calling the model complete.
Drawing arrows that run backwards through the cycle without saying why.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative stage durations and survivorship curves are later work.

relationships: Organisms are enormously varied, and yet all of them share the broad life-cycle pattern of birth, growth, reproduction, and death.
A pattern shared across many kinds of organism is something to be explained, not a coincidence.
A single organism's cycle is an example of the pattern, not the pattern itself.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming that because organisms look different they share nothing.
Treating one organism's particular stages as the pattern that all organisms must follow.
Claiming that a shared pattern means the organisms are the same kind.
topics.out_of_scope: Common ancestry as the explanation for shared patterns is Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Organisms inherit many of their traits from their parents.
Offspring resemble their parents but are not identical to them.
Inheritance passes information from parent to offspring; it does not pass on what happened to the parent during its life.
accepted_alternative_framings: Saying traits are 'passed down' or 'inherited' are both correct at this grade.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming offspring of two parents are identical copies of one parent.
Claiming a trait a parent acquired during life, such as a scar or a learned skill, is inherited.
Claiming every trait an organism has was inherited.
topics.out_of_scope: Genes, chromosomes, dominance, and Punnett squares are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Individuals of the same kind of organism differ from one another, and that difference is called variation.
Variation exists even among siblings that share the same two parents.
Variation is described by comparing many individuals, not by looking at one.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming all members of one kind of organism are the same.
Treating a single individual as representing its whole group.
Claiming variation means the organisms are different kinds.
topics.out_of_scope: Mutation and recombination as the sources of variation are later work.

relationships: Offspring traits can be compared with parent traits to see which are similar and which differ.
A trait can appear in an offspring that neither parent shows.
Resemblance to a parent is evidence of inheritance; it does not establish which parent a particular trait came from.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a trait must have come from whichever parent the offspring most resembles overall.
Claiming a trait absent in both parents cannot have been inherited.
Claiming offspring must show the average of their two parents.
topics.out_of_scope: Recessive inheritance, carriers, and Punnett squares are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Some traits are affected by the environment: food, water, light, temperature, exercise, and injury.
Two organisms with the same inheritance can end up different if they grow in different environments.
An environmental effect on one organism is not passed to its offspring by inheritance.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every difference between two organisms is inherited.
Claiming a trait changed by the environment during an organism's life will be inherited by its offspring.
Claiming the environment has no effect on any trait.
topics.out_of_scope: Gene-environment interaction and epigenetics are later work.

relationships: Trait data from many individuals can be put in a table or graph to show how common each form of the trait is.
The shape of the data, where most individuals fall and how spread out they are, is the evidence; no single individual is.
A graph of trait data shows what was recorded and nothing more.
disqualifying_errors: Drawing a conclusion about the group from one individual's measurement.
Reading the tallest bar as 'all' rather than 'most'.
Claiming a trait is absent from a group because it did not appear in a small sample.
topics.out_of_scope: Mean, median, spread, and the names of distributions are later work.

relationships: A claim about traits is supported by recorded observations of real organisms, or by published records of them.
Evidence has to bear on the claim being made; observations of a different trait do not support it.
The source of an observation is named so that a reader can check it.
disqualifying_errors: Supporting a trait claim with an opinion or a story rather than a recorded observation.
Offering evidence that does not bear on the claim.
Presenting an invented observation as a real one.
topics.out_of_scope: Sampling design and statistical significance are later work.

relationships: Some animals live in groups that vary in size and organisation; others live alone for most of their lives.
Living in a group is a behaviour, and like other traits it varies between kinds of animal.
A group of animals is many organisms together, not one large organism.
accepted_alternative_framings: Herd, flock, school, colony, and pack are all correct names for particular kinds of group.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming all animals of a kind live in groups.
Claiming group living is always the better strategy.
Treating a group of animals as a single organism.
topics.out_of_scope: Kin selection and social-insect caste systems are later work.

relationships: Groups can help members find food, defend against predators, care for young, and cope with harsh conditions.
Group living also has costs, such as competition for food inside the group and faster spread of disease.
Whether group living helps depends on the environment; it is not an advantage everywhere.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming group living has benefits and no costs.
Claiming animals live in groups because they have worked out that it is beneficial.
Claiming a benefit without connecting it to a need the animals actually have.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantitative fitness models and cost-benefit calculations are later work.

relationships: Every organism needs particular resources and conditions: food or nutrients, water, air or dissolved gases, shelter, and space.
A habitat is a place that supplies those needs; an organism cannot survive where its needs are not met.
Different organisms need different things from the same place.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming any organism could live anywhere if it tried hard enough.
Claiming every organism in one habitat needs the same resources.
Listing only food as a habitat need.
topics.out_of_scope: Niche theory and tolerance curves are later work.

relationships: In a particular habitat, some variations of a trait help an individual survive and reproduce better than other variations do.
The same trait can be an advantage in one habitat and a disadvantage in another.
Surviving well means surviving and reproducing, not being the largest or the strongest.
disqualifying_errors: Calling a trait better without naming the habitat it is better in.
Claiming an organism develops a trait because it needs it.
Claiming the strongest individual always survives.
topics.out_of_scope: Natural selection as a mechanism acting over generations is Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: A scientific argument states a claim, gives evidence, and explains how the evidence supports the claim.
The reasoning step is what connects evidence to claim; without it the argument is a claim with data sitting beside it.
An argument is judged on the fit between claim, evidence, and reasoning, not on how strongly it is stated.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a claim and data with no reasoning linking them.
Giving reasoning that does not use the evidence presented.
Treating confident wording as a substitute for evidence.
topics.out_of_scope: Counter-argument and rebuttal structure are later work.

relationships: Evidence for a survival claim names the habitat, names the trait, and connects the trait to a need in that habitat.
Evidence can come from the learner's own observation or from a named published source.
A survival claim covers the habitat the evidence came from, not every habitat.
disqualifying_errors: Supporting a survival claim with a trait that has no stated connection to a need in that habitat.
Using an invented example as evidence.
Extending a survival claim to habitats the evidence never covered.
topics.out_of_scope: Field-study design and population data analysis are later work.

fixed_facts: A fossil is preserved evidence of an organism that lived in the past.
relationships: A fossil is preserved evidence of an organism that lived in the past: a body part, an impression, or a trace such as a footprint or burrow.
Most fossils form in sedimentary rock, when remains are buried by sediment before they decay away.
Only a very small fraction of organisms ever become fossils, so the fossil record is incomplete.
accepted_alternative_framings: Body fossils and trace fossils are both fossils; a learner who names only one kind is not wrong unless they deny the other.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a fossil is the organism's actual unchanged body.
Claiming the fossil record contains every organism that ever lived.
Claiming a rock that merely looks like an organism is a fossil.
topics.out_of_scope: Mineral replacement chemistry, taphonomy, and index fossils are later work.

fixed_facts: In undisturbed sedimentary layers, a lower layer is older than a layer above it.
relationships: Sedimentary rock forms in layers, with newer layers deposited on top of older ones.
In undisturbed layers, a lower layer is older than the layer above it.
Layers can be tilted, folded, or broken after they form, so whether a sequence is undisturbed has to be checked rather than assumed.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the top layer is the oldest.
Claiming the order of layers gives an age in years.
Applying the deeper-is-older rule to layers that have visibly been tilted or overturned without saying so.
topics.out_of_scope: Radiometric dating and the stratigraphic principles by their formal names are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Fossils are evidence about which organisms lived in a place and about the conditions there.
A fossil in a rock layer shows the organism lived when that layer was forming, not when the fossil was found.
Similar fossils in layers of the same age in different places link those places in time.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a body fossil shows what the organism did; only trace fossils record behaviour.
Claiming that finding no fossils of an organism proves it never lived there.
Dating a fossil by when it was collected rather than by the layer it came from.
topics.out_of_scope: Biostratigraphic correlation and continental drift are later work.

fixed_facts: Fossils of sea organisms in rock far from any sea are evidence that the area was once under water.
relationships: Fossils of organisms that live in particular conditions today are evidence that similar conditions existed where those fossils formed.
Marine fossils found far inland are evidence that the area was once covered by water.
Environments change over long spans of time.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming the environment where a fossil is found today must always have been the same.
Concluding what a whole region was like from one fossil.
Claiming an environment cannot change.
topics.out_of_scope: Palaeoclimate proxies and isotope evidence are High School work.

fixed_facts: Extinct means no members of that kind of organism are alive anywhere.
People did not live alongside the large non-bird dinosaurs.
relationships: Some fossil organisms resemble organisms alive today; others resemble nothing now living.
Organisms known only as fossils are extinct: none are alive anywhere.
A resemblance between a fossil and a living organism is evidence of similarity, not proof that one descended from the other.
disqualifying_errors: Treating 'it might still be alive somewhere' as a scientific conclusion about an extinct organism.
Claiming a fossil organism turned into a living organism during its own lifetime.
Claiming people lived alongside the large non-bird dinosaurs.
topics.out_of_scope: Evolutionary relationship and common ancestry are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Individuals in a past population varied, just as individuals do today.
A variation that helped individuals survive and reproduce in their environment could become more common in later generations.
Which variation counts as an advantage is set by the environment, not by the organism.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming an individual organism changes its own traits to suit its environment.
Claiming a trait appeared because the organism needed it.
Claiming an advantage in one environment is an advantage everywhere.
topics.out_of_scope: The mechanism of natural selection and the genetics behind it are Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: Weather is the state of the atmosphere at a place at a particular time: temperature, precipitation, wind, and cloud.
Weather is recorded with instruments, in units, at a stated time and place.
A single day's weather does not describe what a place's weather is usually like.
disqualifying_errors: Recording a weather observation with no date, time, or place.
Concluding what a place's weather is usually like from one day's record.
Recording a temperature with no unit.
topics.out_of_scope: Instrument calibration and station-siting standards are later work.

relationships: A table organises weather data so values can be compared; a graph shows the pattern in those values.
A graph needs labelled axes with units, or a reader cannot tell what is shown.
A graph shows what was recorded; it does not add information that was never measured.
accepted_alternative_framings: Bar graphs and line graphs are both correct choices here, provided the graph type suits the data.
disqualifying_errors: Reading a trend off a graph with unlabelled axes.
Extending a graph beyond the data and treating the extension as a measurement.
Changing a plotted value so the graph looks smoother.
topics.out_of_scope: Line of best fit, interpolation, and correlation are later work.

fixed_facts: When it is summer in the Northern Hemisphere it is winter in the Southern Hemisphere.
relationships: At most places, weather varies in a repeating yearly pattern of seasons.
A seasonal pattern is found by comparing records across several years, not one year.
The seasons in the Northern and Southern Hemispheres are opposite to each other at the same time of year.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming seasons happen because Earth is closer to the Sun in summer.
Claiming every year's weather matches the seasonal average exactly.
Claiming the whole world has summer at the same time.
topics.out_of_scope: The tilt of Earth's axis as the mechanism is Grade 5 and Grade 8 work and is not required here; a learner who states it correctly is right.

fixed_facts: Climate is the long-term pattern of weather at a place, described over many years.
relationships: Weather is short-term and local; climate is the pattern of weather at a place over many years.
One cold day does not contradict a warm climate, and one hot week is not a change in climate.
Climate is described with long-term averages and ranges, not single readings.
disqualifying_errors: Using a single day's weather as evidence about climate.
Treating weather and climate as the same thing.
Claiming climate never changes.
topics.out_of_scope: Climate classification systems and attribution of climate change are later work.

relationships: Different regions of the world have different climates.
Climate varies with distance from the equator, height above sea level, and nearness to large bodies of water.
Two places at the same distance from the equator can have different climates because of those other factors.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming distance from the equator alone determines climate.
Claiming every place near the equator is a rainforest.
Claiming a mountain top and the valley below it must share a climate because they are close together.
topics.out_of_scope: Ocean currents and prevailing winds as mechanisms, and formal climate classes, are later work.

relationships: A conclusion about weather or climate is stronger when it draws on more than one record or source.
Each source is named so a reader can check it.
Sources that disagree are information in themselves; the disagreement is reported, not hidden.
disqualifying_errors: Presenting a combined conclusion with no sources named.
Dropping a source because it disagrees with the others.
Treating two copies of the same source as two independent sources.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighting and formal reconciliation of conflicting datasets are later work.

relationships: Weather-related hazards include floods, severe thunderstorms, tornadoes, blizzards, drought, and extreme heat and cold.
A hazard is a natural event; it becomes a disaster when it affects people or the things they depend on.
Hazards cannot be stopped from happening, but their impacts can be reduced.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming a weather hazard can be prevented from occurring.
Claiming hazards are entirely unpredictable; many have known seasons, regions, and warning signs.
Claiming a hazard is a disaster regardless of whether anyone is affected.
topics.out_of_scope: Probabilistic risk assessment and return periods are later work.

relationships: When a habitat changes, some organisms survive there, some move away, and some die.
Changes can be sudden, such as a flood or fire, or gradual, such as a long drought.
A change that harms one kind of organism can help another.
disqualifying_errors: Claiming every habitat change harms every organism in it.
Claiming individual organisms adapt themselves to fit a changed habitat.
Claiming a habitat that has changed can never support life again.
topics.out_of_scope: Population-level change across generations is Grade 8 and High School work.

relationships: A hazard-reduction design states what it must achieve, which are its criteria, and the limits it must respect, which are its constraints, including safety and cost.
The problem is defined before solutions are generated.
A design that breaks a stated constraint has not solved the problem, however well it meets the criteria.
disqualifying_errors: Proposing a solution before stating what it has to achieve.
Ignoring a stated constraint and still calling the design successful.
Treating safety as an optional constraint.
topics.out_of_scope: Formal engineering standards and building codes are later work.

relationships: Solutions are compared against the same criteria and the same constraints.
A solution can be better on one criterion and worse on another, and the comparison says so.
The comparison reports what was tested, not what was hoped for.
disqualifying_errors: Declaring a solution best without stating the criteria used.
Comparing two solutions against different criteria.
Ignoring a criterion on which the preferred solution does badly.
topics.out_of_scope: Weighted decision matrices and formal trade studies are later work.

relationships: A design test changes one thing at a time and holds the rest the same, exactly as any fair test does.
A test that shows a design failing is useful evidence and points to the revision.
The test has to measure what the criterion states, not whatever is easiest to measure.
disqualifying_errors: Changing the design and the test conditions at the same time and crediting the difference to the design.
Treating a failed test as a reason to stop rather than as evidence for revision.
Measuring something other than what the criterion states and reporting it as the criterion.
topics.out_of_scope: Statistical comparison of design variants is later work.

relationships: A claim about a hazard or a design is supported by recorded data or by a named source.
The reasoning states how the evidence supports the claim.
A claim broader than the evidence covers is overstated and should be narrowed to what was actually shown.
disqualifying_errors: Making a claim broader than the evidence collected supports.
Presenting an untested design as proven.
Citing no source and no data for a factual claim.
topics.out_of_scope: Quantified uncertainty and confidence statements are later work.
